claim: Plant leaves constitute a huge microbial habitat of global importance.
source: Plant leaves constitute a huge microbial habitat of global importance.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the phyllosphere as a microbial habitat.

claim: How microorganisms survive the dry daytime on leaves and avoid desiccation is not well understood.
source: How microorganisms survive the dry daytime on leaves and avoid desiccation is not well understood.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current scientific understanding.

claim: Microscopic surface wetness in the form of thin films and micrometer-sized droplets, invisible to the naked eye, persists on leaves during daytime due to deliquescence.
source: There is evidence that microscopic surface wetness in the form of thin films and micrometer-sized droplets, invisible to the naked eye, persists on leaves during daytime due to deliquescence – the absorption of water until dissolution – of hygroscopic aerosols.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to existing evidence in the literature.

claim: On surfaces drying under moderate humidity, stable microdroplets form around bacterial aggregates due to capillary pinning and deliquescence.
source: We show that, on surfaces drying under moderate humidity, stable microdroplets form around bacterial aggregates due to capillary pinning and deliquescence.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental observations.

claim: Droplet-size increases with aggregate-size.
source: Notably, droplet-size increases with aggregate-size, and cell survival is higher the larger the droplet.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantitative analysis shown in the manuscript.

claim: Cell survival is higher the larger the droplet.
source: Notably, droplet-size increases with aggregate-size, and cell survival is higher the larger the droplet.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by survival assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Microdroplet formation around aggregates was observed for 13 bacterial species.
source: This phenomenon was observed for 13 bacterial species, two of which – Pseudomonas fluorescens and P. putida – were studied in depth.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from multiple bacterial strains listed in Table 1.

claim: Pseudomonas fluorescens and P. putida were studied in depth.
source: This phenomenon was observed for 13 bacterial species, two of which – Pseudomonas fluorescens and P. putida – were studied in depth.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the experimental design.

claim: Microdroplet formation around aggregates is likely key to bacterial survival in a variety of unsaturated microbial habitats, including leaf surfaces.
source: Microdroplet formation around aggregates is likely key to bacterial survival in a variety of unsaturated microbial habitats, including leaf surfaces.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The phyllosphere is a vast microbial habitat that is home to diverse microbial communities.
source: The phyllosphere – the aerial parts of plants – is a vast microbial habitat that is home to diverse microbial communities (Lindow and Brandl, 2003; Lindow and Leveau, 2002; Vorholt, 2012; Vacher et al., 2016; Leveau, 2015; Bringel and CouÃce, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Phyllosphere microbial communities are dominated by bacteria.
source: These communities, dominated by bacteria, play a major role in the function and health of their host plant, and take part in global biogeochemical cycles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about phyllosphere microbial communities.

claim: Phyllosphere microbial communities play a major role in the function and health of their host plant.
source: These communities, dominated by bacteria, play a major role in the function and health of their host plant, and take part in global biogeochemical cycles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the ecological importance of phyllosphere microbes.

claim: Phyllosphere microbial communities take part in global biogeochemical cycles.
source: These communities, dominated by bacteria, play a major role in the function and health of their host plant, and take part in global biogeochemical cycles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the global ecological role of phyllosphere microbes.

claim: Hydration conditions on plant leaf surfaces vary considerably over the diurnal cycle, typically with wet nights and dry days.
source: Hydration conditions on plant leaf surfaces vary considerably over the diurnal cycle, typically with wet nights and dry days (Beattie, 2011; Brewer and Smith, 1997; Magarey et al., 2005; Klemm et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Leaf surfaces are frequently covered by thin liquid films or micrometer-sized droplets that are invisible to the naked eye during the day.
source: While leaf surfaces may appear to be completely dry during the day, there is increasing evidence that they are frequently covered by thin liquid films or micrometer-sized droplets that are invisible to the naked eye (Burkhardt and Hunsche, 2013; Burkhardt and Eiden, 1994; Burkhardt et al., 2001) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Microscopic wetness on leaves results, in large part, from the deliquescence of hygroscopic particles.
source: This microscopic wetness results, in large part, from the deliquescence of hygroscopic particles that absorb moisture until they dissolve in the absorbed water and form a solution.
evidence: This is an explanation based on established physical-chemical principles.

claim: Aerosols are one ubiquitous source of deliquescent compounds on plant leaf surfaces.
source: One ubiquitous source of deliquescent compounds on plant leaf surfaces is aerosols (Pöschl, 2005; Tang and Munkelwitz, 1993; Tang, 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on aerosols.

claim: During the day, the relative humidity in the boundary layer close to the leaf surface is typically higher than that in the surrounding air, due to transpiration through open stomata.
source: Notably, during the day, the relative humidity (RH) in the boundary layer close to the leaf surface is typically higher than that in the surrounding air, due to transpiration through open stomata.
evidence: This is established knowledge about leaf physiology and microclimate.

claim: When RH is above the deliquescent point, highly concentrated solutions form in the form of thin films and microscopic droplets.
source: Thus, in many cases, the RH is above the deliquescent point, leading to the formation of highly concentrated solutions in the form of thin films (<a few µm) and microscopic droplets (Burkhardt and Hunsche, 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on physical-chemical principles and supported by a citation.

claim: The phenomenon of deliquescence-associated microscopic surface wetness is under-studied.
source: The phenomenon of deliquescence-associated microscopic surface wetness is under-studied, and little is known about its impact on microbial ecology of the phyllosphere and on its contribution to desiccation avoidance and cell survival during the dry daytime.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge.

claim: Little is known about the impact of microscopic surface wetness on microbial ecology of the phyllosphere.
source: The phenomenon of deliquescence-associated microscopic surface wetness is under-studied, and little is known about its impact on microbial ecology of the phyllosphere and on its contribution to desiccation avoidance and cell survival during the dry daytime.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge.

claim: Microscopic hydration conditions around bacterial cells are expected to significantly affect cell survival in soil, root, and leaf surfaces.
source: The microscopic hydration conditions around bacterial cells are expected to significantly affect cell survival in the largest terrestrial microbial habitats – soil, root, and leaf surfaces – that experience recurring wet-dry cycles.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on logical inference from known principles.

claim: Only a few studies have attempted to characterize the microscopic hydration conditions surrounding cells on a drying surface under moderate RH.
source: Only a few studies have attempted to characterize the microscopic hydration conditions surrounding cells on a drying surface under moderate RH and the involvement of deliquescent substrates in this process.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific literature.

claim: Bacterial survival in deliquescent wetness has mainly been studied in extremely dry deserts and on Mars analog environments.
source: Bacterial survival in deliquescent wetness has mainly been studied in extremely dry deserts (Davila et al., 2008; Davila et al., 2013) and on Mars analog environments (Nuding et al., 2017; Stevens et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Soft liquid-like substances wrapped around cells, whose formation was suggested to be due to deliquescence of solute components, were reported.
source: Soft liquid-like substances wrapped around cells, whose formation was suggested to be due to deliquescence of solute components, were reported (Méndez-Vilas et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The interplay between droplet formation, bacterial surface colonization, and survival has not been studied systematically.
source: Yet, the interplay between droplet formation, bacterial surface colonization, and survival, has not been studied systematically.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge.

claim: The majority of bacterial cells on leaf surfaces are typically found within surface-attached aggregates, that is biofilms.
source: The majority of cells are typically found within surface-attached aggregates, that is biofilms (Monier and Lindow, 2004; Morris et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Increased survival rate in aggregates under dry conditions on leaves has been reported.
source: This is consistent with the reported increased survival rate in aggregates under dry conditions on leaves, and poor survival of solitary cells (Monier and Lindow, 2003; Rigano et al., 2007; Yu et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Poor survival of solitary cells under dry conditions on leaves has been reported.
source: This is consistent with the reported increased survival rate in aggregates under dry conditions on leaves, and poor survival of solitary cells (Monier and Lindow, 2003; Rigano et al., 2007; Yu et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The conventional explanation for the increased survival in aggregates is the protective role of the extracellular polymeric substances (EPS), a matrix that acts as a hydrogel.
source: The conventional explanation for the increased survival in aggregates is the protective role of the extracellular polymeric substances (EPS), a matrix that acts as a hydrogel (Chang et al., 2007; Or et al., 2007; Roberson and Firestone, 1992; Ophir and Gutnick, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The resulting microscale hydration conditions around cells on a drying surface depend on cellular organization.
source: We hypothesize that the resulting microscale hydration conditions around cells on a drying surface depend on cellular organization (i.e. solitary/aggregated cells and aggregate size) and that the microscale hydration conditions (i.e. droplet size) affect cell survival.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors.

claim: Microscale hydration conditions (i.e. droplet size) affect cell survival.
source: We hypothesize that the resulting microscale hydration conditions around cells on a drying surface depend on cellular organization (i.e. solitary/aggregated cells and aggregate size) and that the microscale hydration conditions (i.e. droplet size) affect cell survival.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors.

claim: At 85% RH, it took about 14 ± 1 hr for the bulk water to evaporate.
source: At 85% RH, it took about 14 ± 1 hr for the bulk water to evaporate.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: During evaporation, some cells attached to the surface and, over time, grew and formed aggregates for both P. fluorescens and P. putida.
source: During this time, for both studied strains, some of the cells attached to the surface and, over time, grew and formed aggregates.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Some cells formed cell clusters at the liquid-air interface (pellicles).
source: Other cells formed cell clusters at the liquid-air interface (pellicles).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: The glass substrate appeared dry to the naked eye after 14 ± 1 hr of incubation.
source: The glass substrate appeared dry to the naked eye after 14 ± 1 hr of incubation.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: The surface was covered by stable microscopic droplets, mainly around bacterial aggregates.
source: Remarkably, the surface was covered by stable microscopic droplets, mainly around bacterial aggregates (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by microscopy images in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Solitary cells were surrounded by miniscule droplets.
source: Notably, while solitary cells were surrounded by miniscule droplets (possibly similar to those reported by Méndez-Vilas et al., 2011), larger aggregates (of ~100 cells) were surrounded by large droplets measuring tens of µm in diameter.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Larger aggregates (of ~100 cells) were surrounded by large droplets measuring tens of µm in diameter.
source: Notably, while solitary cells were surrounded by miniscule droplets (possibly similar to those reported by Méndez-Vilas et al., 2011), larger aggregates (of ~100 cells) were surrounded by large droplets measuring tens of µm in diameter.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Microscopic wetness was retained around bacterial cells for more than 24 hr.
source: Microscopic wetness was retained around bacterial cells for more than 24 hr, while uncolonized surface areas appeared completely dry.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Uncolonized surface areas appeared completely dry.
source: Microscopic wetness was retained around bacterial cells for more than 24 hr, while uncolonized surface areas appeared completely dry.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Droplet size follows a power law distribution for both P. fluorescens and P. putida.
source: We found that droplet size (measured by droplet area) follows a power law distribution with similar exponents for the two studied strains (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The power law exponent for P. fluorescens droplet size distribution is γ = −1.2 ± 0.15.
source: (C) Droplet-size distributions at 24 hr: Droplets from both strains show power law distributions with relatively similar exponents (γ = −1.2 ± 0.15 (mean ± SEM) and −1.0 ± 0.45 for P. fluorescens and P. putida, respectively).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from data analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The power law exponent for P. putida droplet size distribution is γ = −1.0 ± 0.45.
source: (C) Droplet-size distributions at 24 hr: Droplets from both strains show power law distributions with relatively similar exponents (γ = −1.2 ± 0.15 (mean ± SEM) and −1.0 ± 0.45 for P. fluorescens and P. putida, respectively).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from data analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A clear positive correlation between cell abundance and droplet size emerged.
source: When droplet size was plotted as a function of area covered by cells within each droplet (as a proxy for cell number - see Materials and methods), a clear positive correlation between cell abundance and droplet size emerged (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Experiments using hydrophobic polystyrene substrate rather than glass yielded qualitatively similar results.
source: Experiments using hydrophobic polystyrene substrate rather than glass also yielded qualitatively similar results (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Microdroplets formed even around fluorescent beads (2 µm in diameter).
source: First, we repeated the experiments with fluorescent beads (2 µm in diameter) instead of bacteria. Interestingly, we found that microdroplets formed even around beads (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) with a similar droplet-size distribution, as in experiments with bacteria; and a surprisingly similar correlation between the size of the droplet and the number of beads therein (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Experiments with beads showed a similar droplet-size distribution as experiments with bacteria.
source: Interestingly, we found that microdroplets formed even around beads (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) with a similar droplet-size distribution, as in experiments with bacteria; and a surprisingly similar correlation between the size of the droplet and the number of beads therein (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data shown in Figures 2C-D.

claim: Experiments with beads showed a similar correlation between the size of the droplet and the number of beads therein as experiments with bacteria.
source: Interestingly, we found that microdroplets formed even around beads (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) with a similar droplet-size distribution, as in experiments with bacteria; and a surprisingly similar correlation between the size of the droplet and the number of beads therein (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by data shown in Figures 2C-D.

claim: In a control experiment without any particulates, a much smaller number of droplets formed (<1 droplets of >10 µm2 area per mm2).
source: In a control experiment without any particulates – bacterial cells or beads – a much smaller number of droplets formed (<1 droplets of >10 µm2 area per mm2, as opposed to >100 droplets of that size in experiments with bacteria).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from a control experiment.

claim: The presence of particles is necessary for droplet formation.
source: These results indicate that the presence of particles is necessary for droplet formation, whereas biological activity is not.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental results with beads and controls.

claim: Biological activity is not necessary for droplet formation.
source: These results indicate that the presence of particles is necessary for droplet formation, whereas biological activity is not.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental results with beads.

claim: In experiments with beads in pure water instead of M9 medium, no droplets were observed.
source: Last, we repeated the beads experiment with pure water instead of M9 medium. This time we did not observe any droplets (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that the solutes control droplet formation and retention through their deliquescent properties.
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Solutes control droplet formation and retention through their deliquescent properties.
source: This time we did not observe any droplets (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that the solutes control droplet formation and retention through their deliquescent properties.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental results with pure water.

claim: Retention of droplets around aggregates as well as solitary cells, through pinning of the liquid-air interface, is clearly evident in time-lapse imaging.
source: To observe the surface's final drying phase, we used time-lapse imaging, enabling us to capture the receding front of the remaining thin liquid layer and the formation of microdroplets. Retention of droplets around aggregates as well as solitary cells, through pinning of the liquid-air interface, is clearly evident (Figure 2E, Videos 1–3).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by time-lapse imaging data in Figure 2E and Videos 1-3.

claim: The cause of pinning is the strong capillary forces acting on the rough surfaces produced by the presence of particulates.
source: The cause of this pinning is the strong capillary forces acting on the rough surfaces produced by the presence of particulates (Bonn et al., 2009; Herminghaus et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an explanation based on physical principles and supported by citations.

claim: Aggregate sizes (but possibly also other properties) determine droplet size.
source: This phenomenon supports the notion that aggregate sizes (but possibly also other properties) determine droplet size.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Under the experimental conditions, the droplets were not formed through the wetting 'direction' of a deliquescence process, by which solid salts absorb water until dissolution.
source: We note that under our experimental conditions, the droplets were not formed through the wetting 'direction' of a deliquescence process, by which solid salts absorb water until dissolution.
evidence: This is a clarification about the mechanism of droplet formation in the experiments.

claim: The deliquescent properties of the solutes prevented complete evaporation at RH above the point of deliquescence of the salts mixture.
source: Rather, the deliquescent properties of the solutes prevented complete evaporation at RH above the point of deliquescence of the salts mixture.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism of droplet retention based on physical-chemical principles.

claim: Both particulates and deliquescent solutes are essential for the differential formation and retention of microscopic wetness around cells and aggregates.
source: In summary, both particulates and deliquescent solutes are essential for the differential formation and retention of microscopic wetness around cells and aggregates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The microdroplet solution is estimated to be 23.3 ± 3.5 (mean ± SD) more concentrated than a standard M9.
source: We found that the microdroplet solution is highly concentrated – as can be expected from deliquescent wetness – and is estimated to be 23.3 ± 3.5 (mean ± SD) more concentrated than a standard M9 (~50 times more concentrated than the diluted 0.5x M9 used in our experiments) (See Materials and methods, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement supported by calibration experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The microdroplet solution is ~50 times more concentrated than the diluted 0.5x M9 used in the experiments.
source: We found that the microdroplet solution is highly concentrated – as can be expected from deliquescent wetness – and is estimated to be 23.3 ± 3.5 (mean ± SD) more concentrated than a standard M9 (~50 times more concentrated than the diluted 0.5x M9 used in our experiments) (See Materials and methods, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement derived from the concentration factor.

claim: The high estimated mean osmolarity within the droplets (~6.7 Osm/L) likely imposes severe osmotic stress on cells within them.
source: The high estimated mean osmolarity within the droplets (~6.7 Osm/L, see Supplementary file 1) likely imposes severe osmotic stress on cells within them.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured concentration and known effects of osmotic stress.

claim: Growth curves of P. fluorescens and P. putida in liquid cultures of equivalent concentrated M9 and M9+NaCl media showed delayed or complete growth inhibition.
source: Indeed, growth curves of the two strains (P. fluorescens and P. putida) in liquid cultures of equivalent concentrated M9 and M9+NaCl media showed delayed or complete growth inhibition (Figure 3—figure supplement 5, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by growth curve data in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: Cell divisions within droplets was rarely seen at 85% RH.
source: This result accords with the observation that cell divisions within droplets was rarely seen in our experiments (at 85% RH).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Survival of cells was nearly exclusively restricted to large droplets for both strains (>103 µm2 area).
source: Notably, although the overall population distribution along droplet size was strain specific, survival of cells was nearly exclusively restricted to large droplets for both strains (>103 µm2 area; Figure 3C,D, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by survival assay data shown in Figures 3C-D.

claim: P. putida showed higher overall survival than did P. fluorescens (16% vs. 7%, 24 hr after drying).
source: P. putida showed higher overall survival than did P. fluorescens (16% vs. 7%, 24 hr after drying).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from survival assays.

claim: The overall survival often varied between experiments, and in some cases P. fluorescens had higher survival than did P. putida.
source: We note that the overall survival often varied between experiments, and in some cases P. fluorescens had higher survival than did P. putida.
evidence: This is an observation about experimental variability.

claim: The fraction of live cells within droplets increases with droplet size for both strains.
source: Importantly, regardless of this stochasticity, common to all experiments was a clear trend for both strains: The fraction of live cells within droplets increases with droplet size (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Survival probabilities in small droplets (<102 µm2 area) were poor (<5%).
source: Accordingly, survival probabilities in small droplets (<102 µm2 area) were poor (<5%), in contrast to >50% survival of both strains in the largest droplets (>104 µm2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from survival assays.

claim: Survival of both strains in the largest droplets (>104 µm2) was >50%.
source: Accordingly, survival probabilities in small droplets (<102 µm2 area) were poor (<5%), in contrast to >50% survival of both strains in the largest droplets (>104 µm2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from survival assays.

claim: For both strains, droplet size strongly affects survival, whereas aggregate size has only a marginal (P. fluorescens) or moderate (P. putida) effect on survival.
source: Analysis of cell survival rates as a function of both aggregate size (which by itself affects survival; Monier and Lindow, 2003, cf. Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and the size of the droplet they inhabit, shows that for both strains, droplet size strongly affects survival, whereas aggregate size has only a marginal (P. fluorescens) or moderate (P. putida) effect on survival (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data analysis shown in Figures 3F-G.

claim: A multinomial logistic regression model gave significantly higher weight to droplet size in comparison to aggregate size, for both strains.
source: The relative contribution of each of these two variables was also assessed by a multinomial logistic regression model, giving significantly higher weight to droplet size in comparison to aggregate size, for both strains (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from statistical modeling shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: In experiments where cells were inoculated at a later stage and were mostly solitary, live cells were observed nearly exclusively in large droplets (>103 µm2 area).
source: To further study droplet size effect on survival, we repeated the drying experiment, but inoculated the cells into the drying medium only at a later stage – closer to the macroscopic drying stage – so that the cells did not have time to grow and form aggregates, and were thus mostly solitary. Notably, live cells were observed nearly exclusively in large droplets (>103 µm2 area, cf. Figure 3—figure supplement 4), and survival increased with droplet size.
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Large droplets promote cell survival even when aggregates are absent.
source: These results indicate that large droplets promote cell survival even when aggregates are absent.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the late-inoculation experiments.

claim: Experiments with 16 additional strains, including Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria from a variety of microbial habitats, yielded qualitatively similar results.
source: Experiments with 16 additional strains, including Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria from a variety of microbial habitats, yielded qualitatively similar results to those described in the preceding paragraphs (Table 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in Table 1.

claim: For all strains tested, larger droplets were observed around aggregates or surface areas more densely populated by cells.
source: Although not all the strains formed aggregates under our experimental conditions, the general picture was same for all strains: Larger droplets were observed around aggregates or surface areas more densely populated by cells (for strains that did not form aggregates), and higher survival was observed in larger droplets.
evidence: This is a general observation across all tested strains.

claim: For all strains tested, higher survival was observed in larger droplets.
source: Although not all the strains formed aggregates under our experimental conditions, the general picture was same for all strains: Larger droplets were observed around aggregates or surface areas more densely populated by cells (for strains that did not form aggregates), and higher survival was observed in larger droplets.
evidence: This is a general observation across all tested strains.

claim: Stable microdroplets formed around natural microbiota cells using solutes and microbiota extracted from the surface of a natural leaf.
source: Lastly, we repeated our experiments using solutes and microbiota extracted from the surface of a natural leaf. We found that stable microdroplets also formed around natural microbiota cells, in some cases only at higher RH (>85%) or at lower temperatures, suggesting that condensation is involved in microdroplet formation.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from experiments with natural leaf washes.

claim: In some cases with natural leaf washes, microdroplets formed only at higher RH (>85%) or at lower temperatures, suggesting that condensation is involved in microdroplet formation.
source: We found that stable microdroplets also formed around natural microbiota cells, in some cases only at higher RH (>85%) or at lower temperatures, suggesting that condensation is involved in microdroplet formation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from experimental observations with natural leaf washes.

claim: The microscopic wetness from natural leaf wash was visibly similar to those in experiments with inoculated bacteria and a synthetic medium.
source: Furthermore, the microscopic wetness from natural leaf wash was visibly similar to those in our experiments with inoculated bacteria and a synthetic medium (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by images in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Stable microdroplets of concentrated liquid solutions form around cells and aggregates on bacterial-colonized surfaces that are drying under moderate to high RH.
source: Our study demonstrates that stable microdroplets of concentrated liquid solutions form around cells and aggregates on bacterial-colonized surfaces that are drying under moderate to high RH.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study.

claim: Bacterial cell organization on a surface strongly affects the microscopic hydration conditions around cells.
source: We show that bacterial cell organization on a surface strongly affects the microscopic hydration conditions around cells, and that droplet size strongly affects cell survival.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study.

claim: Bacterial aggregation improves hydration by retaining large stable droplets (>tens of µm in diameter) around aggregates.
source: We reveal an additional function of bacterial aggregation: improving hydration by retaining large stable droplets (>tens of µm in diameter) around aggregates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Why survival is enhanced in larger droplets remains an open question.
source: Why survival is enhanced in larger droplets remains an open question.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current study.

claim: Larger droplets provide favorable conditions due to higher water potential.
source: We hypothesize that larger droplets provide favorable conditions due to higher water potential; further research is required to test this hypothesis.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The evaporation dynamics of a drop of a liquid solution is a surprisingly rich and complex physical process.
source: We note that the evaporation dynamics of a drop of a liquid solution – even without bacteria – is a surprisingly rich and complex physical process and a subject of intensive research (de Gennes et al., 2013; Bonn et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about the complexity of the physical process, supported by citations.

claim: Two central mechanisms promote the formation and stability of microdroplets around bacterial aggregates: pinning of the liquid-air interface and the deliquescent property of solutes.
source: Our results point to two central mechanisms promoting the formation and stability of microdroplets around bacterial aggregates: The first is pinning of the liquid-air interface due to the large interfacial tension force associated with the rough surfaces of particulate aggregates (Herminghaus et al., 2008; Bonn et al., 2009), as observed in Videos 1–3. The second is the deliquescent property of solutes that prohibits complete evaporation of the pinned droplets at RH that is higher than the point of deliquescence of the solutes, such that the droplets are in equilibrium with the surrounding humid air.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations and supported by citations.

claim: Bacterial self-organization on surfaces can improve survival in environments with recurrent drying that lead to microscopic wetness.
source: We suggest that bacterial self-organization on surfaces can improve survival in environments with recurrent drying that lead to microscopic wetness.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Aggregation can affect self-organization, and in turn, the resulting waterscape, by increasing the fraction of the population that ends up in large droplets.
source: Aggregation is an important feature that can affect self-organization, and in turn, the resulting waterscape, by increasing the fraction of the population that ends up in large droplets.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The ecological origin of the strains did not always predict their survival rates.
source: Interestingly, the ecological origin of the strains (Table 1) did not always predict their survival rates.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments with multiple strains.

claim: Some phyllospheric bacteria (mostly plant pathogens) exhibited low survival.
source: Some phyllospheric bacteria (mostly plant pathogens) exhibited low survival, soil bacteria exhibited variable survival rates, E. coli exhibited a surprising medium survival, and the aquatic strain P. veronii exhibited high survival.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments with multiple strains.

claim: Soil bacteria exhibited variable survival rates.
source: Some phyllospheric bacteria (mostly plant pathogens) exhibited low survival, soil bacteria exhibited variable survival rates, E. coli exhibited a surprising medium survival, and the aquatic strain P. veronii exhibited high survival.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments with multiple strains.

claim: E. coli exhibited a surprising medium survival.
source: Some phyllospheric bacteria (mostly plant pathogens) exhibited low survival, soil bacteria exhibited variable survival rates, E. coli exhibited a surprising medium survival, and the aquatic strain P. veronii exhibited high survival.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments with multiple strains.

claim: The aquatic strain P. veronii exhibited high survival.
source: Some phyllospheric bacteria (mostly plant pathogens) exhibited low survival, soil bacteria exhibited variable survival rates, E. coli exhibited a surprising medium survival, and the aquatic strain P. veronii exhibited high survival.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments with multiple strains.

claim: Survival in microscopic surface wetness is likely a complex trait that combines physiological adaptation of the individual cell and collective protection that results from self-organization and cooperation.
